decks.title: Structured Query Language — Part 1: Defining Tables and Writing Queries
goals: Tell DDL from DML and choose suitable data types and constraints for a table
Use database and table commands: CREATE, USE, SHOW, DESCRIBE, ALTER and DROP
Write SELECT queries with WHERE, DISTINCT, aliases, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL and ORDER BY, and predict their results

slides.heading: Structured Query Language (SQL)
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **defining tables** and **asking questions** of the data with SELECT.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what SQL is, DDL and DML, data types and constraints, database and table commands, SELECT with WHERE, IN, BETWEEN and LIKE, NULL and ORDER BY
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In the last chapter you met the relational model: data stored in tables of rows and columns. Now we learn the language used to talk to such a database, the Structured Query Language. In this first part we create databases and tables, and then ask questions of the data with the select command. Every result you will see was produced by actually running the query.

slides.heading: Why SQL?
slides.body_md: SQL is the standard language of relational databases such as **MySQL**.

rows: You state **what** data you want; the database decides how to fetch it
The same core commands work in MySQL and other relational databases
One query can filter, sort, group and combine thousands of rows
Many users can work on the same data with keys and constraints keeping it correct

visual.alt: Table of the advantages of SQL: declarative, standard, English-like, powerful, and shared and safe with constraints

slides.narration: SQL is declarative. You describe the data you want, and the database works out how to fetch it. The same core commands work across relational databases, the keywords read almost like English, and a single query can filter, sort, group and combine thousands of rows. Constraints and keys keep shared data correct even when many people use it.

slides.heading: Two kinds of commands: DDL and DML
slides.body_md: Some commands shape the **containers**; others work on the **contents**.

visual.alt: Table comparing DDL, which works on structure with CREATE, ALTER and DROP, and DML, which works on rows with INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT

slides.narration: SQL commands fall into two main groups. Data definition language commands, such as create, alter and drop, build or change the structure of databases and tables. Data manipulation language commands, such as insert, update, delete and select, work on the rows stored inside. A useful test: does the command change the shape of the table, or the data in it?

slides.heading: Data types
slides.body_md: Each column gets a **data type** that decides what it can store.

rows: Variable-length text, up to n characters

visual.alt: Table of MySQL data types: CHAR fixed-length text, VARCHAR variable-length text, INT whole numbers, FLOAT decimal numbers and DATE in year-month-day form, each with an example column

slides.narration: When you create a table, every column needs a data type. Char with a size stores text of a fixed length and pads short values with spaces. Varchar stores text of varying length up to its limit. Int stores whole numbers, float stores numbers with a decimal part, and date stores a calendar date written as year, month and day.

slides.heading: Constraints
slides.body_md: Constraints are rules the database checks on every insert and update.

rows: No two rows may have the same value (several NULLs allowed)
Unique **and** not null; identifies each row; one per table

visual.alt: Table of constraints: NOT NULL requires a value, UNIQUE forbids repeated values, and PRIMARY KEY is unique and not null and identifies each row

slides.narration: Constraints protect the data. Not null forces a value to be entered. Unique stops two rows from having the same value, although several rows may leave it empty. A primary key is both unique and not null, so it identifies each row. A table has only one primary key, such as the roll number of a student.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: creating the STUDENT table
slides.body_md:
```sql
CREATE TABLE STUDENT (
  RollNo INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  Class CHAR(3),
  Stream VARCHAR(12),
  Marks INT,
  City VARCHAR(15),
  ClubID INT
);
```

visual.alt: Design of the STUDENT table: RollNo integer primary key, Name variable text not null, Class fixed three characters, Stream, Marks integer, City and ClubID integer
visual.caption: Design of STUDENT (the structure DESCRIBE STUDENT would report)

slides.narration: Here is the statement that creates our student table. Each column is written with its name and type, separated by commas. Roll number is an integer and the primary key. Name is variable text and cannot be left empty. Class is always three characters, so a fixed char type suits it. The table on the right is the design that the describe command would report.

slides.heading: Working with databases
slides.body_md: A first session: create a database, open it, make a table and look at it.

visual.alt: Flow of database commands: create the database, list databases, use it, create a table, list the tables and describe a table
visual.caption: A first session in MySQL

slides.narration: Before creating tables, you create a database and open it with the use command. Show databases lists the databases on the server, and show tables lists the tables in the database you are using. Describe followed by a table name shows its columns, types and keys. These small commands are often asked as one-mark questions.

slides.heading: Quick check: seeing a table's structure
slides.body_md: Which command shows the columns and types of PRODUCT?
slides.narration: Think of the command that describes a table rather than listing its rows.

slides.heading: Changing and removing structure
slides.body_md: ALTER TABLE changes columns and keys; DROP removes whole tables or databases.

visual.alt: Table of ALTER and DROP commands: add or remove a column, add or remove a primary key, drop a table and drop a database

slides.narration: Once a table exists, alter table changes its structure. You can add or remove a column, and add or remove a primary key. Drop table deletes a table with all its data, and drop database deletes a whole database. These cannot be undone, so they are used with great care.

slides.heading: The STUDENT table we will use

visual.alt: The imagined STUDENT table with eight students: roll number, name, class, stream, marks, city and club number, where two students have no club
visual.caption: STUDENT (imagined data used throughout this chapter)

slides.narration: From here on we use this imagined student table. Eight students from three cities are in three streams. Notice that two students have no club: their club number is empty, which SQL calls null. Keep an eye on those two rows; they behave differently in many queries.

slides.heading: The CLUB table we will use
slides.body_md: ClubID links STUDENT to CLUB.

visual.alt: The imagined CLUB table with four clubs: Robotics, Music, Debate and Chess, with teachers and fees
visual.caption: CLUB

slides.narration: The club table lists four clubs with their teachers and fees. Club number is its primary key, and the same column appears in the student table to show which club each student joined. No student has joined chess yet. We will use this link when we join the two tables in the second part.

slides.heading: SELECT, DISTINCT and aliases
slides.body_md:
```sql
SELECT Name, Marks + 5 AS Revised FROM STUDENT WHERE City = 'Nashik' ORDER BY Name;
```

`SELECT DISTINCT City` shows each city once; `AS` gives a column a new heading; arithmetic such as `Marks + 5` is allowed.

visual.alt: Result of an alias query: the two Nashik students with their marks increased by five under the heading Revised
visual.caption: SELECT Name, Marks + 5 AS Revised FROM STUDENT WHERE City = 'Nashik' ORDER BY Name;

slides.narration: Select chooses columns, and from names the table. You can work out new values with arithmetic, and give them a heading with the word as, which is called an alias. Distinct removes repeated values from the result. Here the two Nashik students are shown with five marks added under the heading revised.

slides.heading: WHERE: choosing rows
slides.body_md:
```sql
SELECT Name, Stream, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks >= 80 AND Stream <> 'Science' ORDER BY Marks DESC;
```

Relational operators: `=`, `<>`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`; logical operators: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`.

visual.alt: Result of a WHERE query with AND: students with at least eighty marks who are not in Science, highest first
visual.caption: SELECT Name, Stream, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks >= 80 AND Stream <> 'Science' ORDER BY Marks DESC;

slides.narration: Where keeps only the rows for which a condition is true. Conditions use relational operators such as equals, not equal to, greater than and less than, joined by and, or and not. This query keeps students with at least eighty marks who are not in the science stream, and sorts them from the highest marks down.

slides.heading: Quick check: a missing value
slides.body_md: Complete the condition that finds students without a club.
slides.narration: Remember that an empty value cannot be compared with the equals sign. Which two words test for it?

slides.heading: IN and BETWEEN
slides.body_md:
```sql
SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90 AND City IN ('Pune', 'Nagpur') ORDER BY Name;
```

`IN (…)` matches any value in a list; `BETWEEN a AND b` includes **both** end values.

visual.alt: Result of a query with BETWEEN and IN: students from Pune or Nagpur with marks from seventy to ninety
visual.caption: SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90 AND City IN ('Pune', 'Nagpur') ORDER BY Name;

slides.narration: In is a short way of writing several equality tests joined by or. Between checks a range, and it includes both end values, so marks of exactly seventy or ninety would count. This query finds students from Pune or Nagpur whose marks lie from seventy to ninety.

slides.heading: LIKE: matching patterns
slides.body_md:
```sql
SELECT PName FROM PRODUCT WHERE PName LIKE '%Box' ORDER BY PName;
```

`%` stands for any number of characters (even none); `_` stands for exactly one character.

visual.alt: Result of a LIKE query on PRODUCT: names ending with Box, that is Geometry Box and Lunch Box
visual.caption: SELECT PName FROM PRODUCT WHERE PName LIKE '%Box' ORDER BY PName;

slides.narration: Like searches text with a pattern. The percent sign stands for any number of characters, and the underscore stands for exactly one character. A pattern of percent followed by Box matches names that end with the word Box. A pattern of four underscores would match names exactly four letters long.

slides.heading: NULL and ORDER BY
slides.body_md:
```sql
SELECT Name, Stream FROM STUDENT WHERE ClubID IS NULL ORDER BY Name;
```

Sort on more than one column: `ORDER BY Class, Marks DESC` (within each class, highest marks first).

visual.alt: Result of an IS NULL query: the two students without a club
visual.caption: SELECT Name, Stream FROM STUDENT WHERE ClubID IS NULL ORDER BY Name;

slides.narration: Null means a value is missing or unknown. Because it is unknown, a comparison with equals is never true, so we test it with is null or is not null. Order by sorts the result, ascending unless you write descending. You can sort on two columns: the second one decides the order within ties of the first.

slides.heading: Sorting on two columns

visual.alt: Result of ORDER BY on two columns: students sorted by class and, within each class, by marks from highest to lowest
visual.caption: SELECT Name, Class, Marks FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Class, Marks DESC;

slides.narration: Here the students are sorted by class first. Inside each class they are sorted by marks from the highest down. Look at class twelve A: Gaurav with ninety five comes before Aarav and Chirag. Always add order by when the order of rows matters, because without it the database may return rows in any order.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: building a query clause by clause
slides.body_md:
Task: names and prices of stationery items whose stock is known, dearest first.

```sql
SELECT PName, Price FROM PRODUCT WHERE Category = 'Stationery' AND Stock IS NOT NULL ORDER BY Price DESC;
```

```text
PName        Price
Sketch Pens  110
Notebook     60
Gel Pen      25
```

visual.alt: Flow of how a query is worked out: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY
visual.caption: How MySQL works out a query (written order differs: SELECT comes first)

slides.narration: Build a query in steps. First the table: product. Then the rows: category must be stationery, and stock must be known, so is not null. Then the columns: name and price. Finally the order: price, descending. The flow shows the order in which the database works out a query, which differs from the order in which we write it.

slides.heading: Quick check: BETWEEN
slides.body_md: Which roll numbers does the BETWEEN query return?
slides.narration: Check each student's marks, and remember whether the end values of the range are included.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: DDL for structure, WHERE for rows, IN and BETWEEN, LIKE patterns, IS NULL, and ORDER BY

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Data definition commands create, alter and drop structure; constraints keep the data correct. Select with where picks rows, using relational and logical operators. In tests a list, between tests a range with both ends included, and like matches patterns. Null is tested with is null, and order by sorts the result.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write keywords in capitals and end each statement with a semicolon; quote text and dates with single quotes: `'Pune'`.
Never write `= NULL`; write `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.
For "output" questions, check every row against every condition and then apply ORDER BY.
DELETE removes rows (DML); DROP removes the table (DDL).

rows: Add `WHERE A.col = B.col`, or the result is a Cartesian product
Changes every row: add the condition

visual.alt: Table of common SQL mistakes and their corrections: IS NULL, HAVING for aggregates, join conditions, and WHERE in UPDATE

slides.narration: A few habits earn easy marks. Quote text values in single quotes and end statements with a semicolon. Remember that between includes its end values. Never compare with equals null. In output questions, test each row against every condition, and only then sort. And keep delete, which removes rows, separate from drop, which removes the table.

decks.title: Structured Query Language — Part 2: Aggregates, Groups, Joins and Changes
goals: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, and explain how they treat NULL
Group rows with GROUP BY and filter groups with HAVING
Join two tables by Cartesian product, equi-join and natural join
Change and remove rows with UPDATE and DELETE

slides.heading: SQL: aggregates, groups, joins and changes
slides.body_md: Part 2 — summarising data, combining two tables, and changing rows.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: aggregate functions, COUNT and NULL, GROUP BY, HAVING, Cartesian product, equi-join and natural join, UPDATE and DELETE
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In the first part each query returned rows from a single table. Now we summarise many rows into a single value, form groups, combine two tables with joins, and change or remove rows. These are the queries that carry the most marks in board papers, so practise each one with the tables we already know.

slides.heading: Aggregate functions

visual.alt: Result of five aggregate functions on STUDENT: 8, 58, 95, 633, 79.125 for count, lowest, highest, total and average
visual.caption: SELECT COUNT(*), MIN(Marks), MAX(Marks), SUM(Marks), AVG(Marks) FROM STUDENT; (MySQL shows the average as 79.1250)

slides.narration: Aggregate functions turn many rows into one value. Count gives the number of rows, minimum and maximum give the smallest and largest values, sum adds them, and average gives their mean. For our eight students the marks run from fifty eight to ninety five. MySQL shows averages with extra zeros after the decimal point.

slides.heading: COUNT and NULL
slides.body_md:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(ClubID), COUNT(DISTINCT ClubID) FROM STUDENT;
```

Aggregates **skip NULL**; only `COUNT(*)` counts every row.

visual.alt: Result comparing COUNT star, COUNT of ClubID and COUNT of distinct ClubID: eight, six and three
visual.caption: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(ClubID), COUNT(DISTINCT ClubID) FROM STUDENT;

slides.narration: Aggregate functions skip null values. Count star counts every row, so it gives eight. Count of club number counts only the six students who have a club. Count distinct counts the different clubs that appear, which is three. The same rule applies to sum and average: an empty value is simply left out.

slides.heading: Quick check: SUM and COUNT with NULL
slides.body_md: What does the stationery query show?
slides.narration: One stationery item has no stock entered. Decide what sum and count do with that row.

slides.heading: GROUP BY

visual.alt: Result of GROUP BY Stream: the number of students and the average marks of Commerce, Humanities and Science
visual.caption: SELECT Stream, COUNT(*), AVG(Marks) FROM STUDENT GROUP BY Stream ORDER BY Stream;

slides.narration: Group by collects rows that share a value into groups, and each aggregate is then worked out once per group. Here we get one row for each stream: how many students it has and their average marks. Columns in the select list should either be the grouping column or inside an aggregate function.

slides.heading: HAVING versus WHERE
slides.body_md: WHERE filters **rows** before grouping; HAVING filters **groups** after grouping.

visual.alt: Table comparing WHERE and HAVING: WHERE works on rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates; HAVING works on groups after grouping and can

slides.narration: Where and having both filter, but at different moments. Where looks at single rows before any groups exist, so it cannot use count or average. Having looks at whole groups after grouping, so it can. A query may use both: first where removes rows, then groups are formed, then having keeps the groups you want.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING together
slides.body_md:
Task: for cities with at least two students outside Commerce, the number of such students and their highest marks.

```sql
SELECT City, COUNT(*), MAX(Marks) FROM STUDENT WHERE Stream <> 'Commerce' GROUP BY City HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY City;
```

visual.alt: Result of worked example 3: cities with at least two non-Commerce students, with the count and highest marks
visual.caption: SELECT City, COUNT(*), MAX(Marks) FROM STUDENT WHERE Stream <> 'Commerce' GROUP BY City HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY City;

slides.narration: Follow the steps. Where first removes the three commerce students, leaving five rows. Group by then forms one group per city: Nagpur has one row, Nashik two and Pune two. Having keeps the cities with at least two rows, so Nagpur is dropped. For each remaining city we see the count and the highest marks: ninety five in Nashik and eighty eight in Pune.

slides.heading: Quick check: the group clause
slides.body_md: Which clause keeps only some groups?
slides.narration: Think about which filter runs after the groups have been formed.

slides.heading: Cartesian product
slides.body_md: `SELECT * FROM STUDENT, CLUB;` pairs **every** student with **every** club.

visual.alt: Table showing that the Cartesian product of STUDENT with 8 rows and 7 columns and CLUB with 4 rows and 4 columns has 32 rows and 11 columns
visual.caption: Rows multiply, columns add

slides.narration: When two tables are listed in from without any condition, every row of the first is paired with every row of the second. This is the Cartesian product. Its degree, the number of columns, is the sum of the two degrees. Its cardinality, the number of rows, is the product of the two cardinalities: eight times four gives thirty two.

slides.heading: Equi-join: matching on a common column
slides.body_md:
```sql
SELECT S.Name, C.ClubName
FROM STUDENT S, CLUB C
WHERE S.ClubID = C.ClubID;
```

visual.caption: Equi-join pairs rows with equal ClubID values

slides.narration: Most of those thirty two pairs make no sense. An equi-join keeps only pairs whose common column values are equal, here club number. Each arrow joins a student to the club with the same number. Chirag has no club, so he finds no partner and drops out. The letters S and C are short aliases for the table names.

slides.heading: Natural join
slides.body_md:
```sql
SELECT PName, SupName, City FROM PRODUCT NATURAL JOIN SUPPLIER WHERE Price < 100 ORDER BY PName;
```

A natural join matches on the column with the **same name** in both tables and shows it **once**.

visual.alt: Result of a natural join of PRODUCT and SUPPLIER for products under one hundred rupees, with supplier name and city
visual.caption: SELECT PName, SupName, City FROM PRODUCT NATURAL JOIN SUPPLIER WHERE Price < 100 ORDER BY PName;

slides.narration: A natural join does the matching for you. It looks for the column with the same name in both tables, here supplier code, and keeps the rows where the values are equal. Unlike an equi-join written with select star, it shows the common column only once. This query lists cheaper products with the name and city of their supplier.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a join with conditions
slides.body_md:
Task: students with more than 80 marks, with their club and its fee, highest fee first.

```sql
SELECT S.Name, C.ClubName, C.Fee FROM STUDENT S, CLUB C WHERE S.ClubID = C.ClubID AND S.Marks > 80 ORDER BY C.Fee DESC, S.Name;
```

visual.alt: Result of worked example 4: students with more than eighty marks, their club and its fee, highest fee first
visual.caption: SELECT S.Name, C.ClubName, C.Fee FROM STUDENT S, CLUB C WHERE S.ClubID = C.ClubID AND S.Marks > 80 ORDER BY C.Fee DESC, S.Name;

slides.narration: Combine a join with other conditions using and. The first condition matches club numbers; the second keeps students with more than eighty marks. We then sort by fee from the highest, and by name when fees are equal. Diya and Hina both belong to the debate club, so the name decides their order.

slides.heading: Quick check: degree and cardinality
slides.body_md: Work out the size of the Cartesian product of STUDENT and CLUB.
slides.narration: Columns add and rows multiply. Use the sizes given in the question.

slides.heading: UPDATE: changing values
slides.body_md:
```sql
UPDATE CLUB SET Fee = Fee + 100 WHERE Fee >= 300;
```

Several columns: `SET Stream = 'Science', Class = '12A'`. Without WHERE, **every** row changes.

visual.alt: Table of club fees before and after an UPDATE that adds one hundred rupees to clubs charging three hundred or more: Robotics 500 to 600 and Music 300 to 400
visual.caption: UPDATE CLUB SET Fee = Fee + 100 WHERE Fee >= 300;

slides.narration: Update changes values in rows that already exist. Set names the column and its new value, which may use the old value, as in fee plus one hundred. Where decides which rows change. Here only the clubs charging three hundred or more go up. Forget the where clause and every row would change, a costly mistake.

slides.heading: DELETE and DROP
slides.body_md: `DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks < 60;` removes matching rows only.

visual.alt: Table comparing DELETE with a condition, DELETE without a condition and DROP TABLE: what each removes, whether the table remains, and whether it is DML or DDL

slides.narration: Delete removes rows. With a where clause it removes only the matching rows; without one it empties the table but keeps it. Drop table is different: it removes the table itself, with its structure and data. Delete belongs to the data manipulation language and drop to the data definition language.

slides.heading: Quick check: rows left after DELETE
slides.body_md: How many students remain after the DELETE?
slides.narration: Find the marks below seventy, remove those rows and count what is left.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Equi-join with `=` in WHERE, or `NATURAL JOIN`

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: aggregates, GROUP BY, HAVING, joins, and UPDATE and DELETE

slides.narration: To sum up: aggregate functions turn many rows into one value and skip nulls, except count star. Group by gives one value per group, and having keeps the groups you want. Joins combine tables: a Cartesian product pairs everything, while equi and natural joins keep matching rows. Update and delete change or remove rows chosen by where.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Aggregates in a condition go in **HAVING**, never in WHERE.
Cartesian product: degree = sum of degrees; cardinality = product of cardinalities.
Always write the join condition, and prefix shared column names: `S.ClubID`.

sections.heading: 1. SQL, DDL and DML; data types and constraints
sections.body_md:
SQL is the standard, declarative language of relational databases such as MySQL.

- **DDL** (structure): `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`.
- **DML** (rows): `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `SELECT`.

**Data types:** `CHAR(n)` fixed length (padded), `VARCHAR(n)` variable length, `INT`, `FLOAT`, `DATE` ('YYYY-MM-DD').

**Constraints:** `NOT NULL` (value required), `UNIQUE` (no repeats; several NULLs allowed), `PRIMARY KEY` (unique and not null; one per table).

key_terms.definition_md: Commands that define or change the structure of databases and tables: CREATE, ALTER, DROP.
Commands that insert, change, delete or retrieve rows: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT.
A rule on a column that the database enforces, such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY.

sections.heading: 3. SELECT with WHERE, IN, BETWEEN and LIKE
sections.body_md:
General form: `SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY column;`

- `*` selects all columns; `DISTINCT` removes repeated rows; `AS` gives an alias; arithmetic (`Price * Stock`) is allowed.
- Relational: `=`, `<>`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`; logical: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`.
- `IN ('Pune', 'Nashik')` matches any value in the list; `BETWEEN 70 AND 90` includes both ends.
- `LIKE`: `%` any run of characters, `_` exactly one character.

```sql
SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90 AND City IN ('Pune', 'Nagpur') ORDER BY Name;
```

```text

Aarav   88
Bhavna  74
Farah   79

```

A LIKE symbol: % for any number of characters, _ for exactly one.

sections.heading: 4. NULL and ORDER BY
sections.body_md:
NULL means missing or unknown. Any comparison with NULL using `=` or `<>` is never true, so test with **IS NULL** or **IS NOT NULL**.

`ORDER BY` sorts ascending by default; `DESC` sorts descending. With two columns, the second sorts within ties of the first. In ascending order MySQL puts NULL first.

```sql
SELECT PName, Stock FROM PRODUCT ORDER BY Stock DESC;
```

```text
PName            Stock
Gel Pen          300
Notebook         120
Sketch Pens      80
Water Bottle     45
Lunch Box        30
Extension Board  20
Desk Lamp        12
Geometry Box     NULL
```

In descending order the NULL stock comes last.

sections.heading: 5. Aggregate functions, GROUP BY and HAVING
sections.body_md:
`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` give one value from many rows and **skip NULL** (only `COUNT(*)` counts every row). MySQL shows averages with decimal places (for example 85.0000).

`GROUP BY col` gives one result row per group; `HAVING` filters groups and may use aggregates; `WHERE` filters rows before grouping and may not.

Written order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY.

```sql
SELECT City, COUNT(*), MAX(Marks) FROM STUDENT WHERE Stream <> 'Commerce' GROUP BY City HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY City;
```

```text
City    COUNT(*)  MAX(Marks)
Nashik  2         95
Pune    2         88
```

key_terms.definition_md: A function that returns one value from a set of rows: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
The clause that keeps only the groups satisfying a condition, written after GROUP BY.

sections.heading: 6. Joins, UPDATE and DELETE
sections.body_md:
**Cartesian product:** `SELECT * FROM A, B;` pairs every row of A with every row of B. Degree = degree(A) + degree(B); cardinality = cardinality(A) × cardinality(B).

**Equi-join:** `WHERE A.col = B.col`; the common column appears twice with `SELECT *`.

**Natural join:** `A NATURAL JOIN B` matches the column with the same name and shows it once.

```sql
SELECT S.Name, C.ClubName, C.Fee FROM STUDENT S, CLUB C WHERE S.ClubID = C.ClubID AND S.Marks > 80 ORDER BY C.Fee DESC, S.Name;
```

```text
Name    ClubName  Fee
Gaurav  Robotics  500
Aarav   Music     300
Diya    Debate    200
Hina    Debate    200
```

**UPDATE** `table SET col = value WHERE …;` changes rows; **DELETE FROM** `table WHERE …;` removes rows (all rows without WHERE; the table remains).

key_terms.definition_md: A join that keeps pairs of rows with equal values in the joining columns.
A join on the column with the same name in both tables, which appears once in the result.
The number of rows of a table or result; degree is the number of columns.

questions.stem_md: Which one of these SQL commands belongs to the **Data Definition Language (DDL)**?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** `ALTER TABLE`. DDL commands create or change the structure of database objects: CREATE, ALTER and DROP. INSERT, UPDATE and SELECT work on the data stored in tables, so they are DML commands.

questions.stem_md: The office of an imagined school wants to change the city of a student whose record is already stored in the STUDENT table. Which category of command and which command should it use?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** DML, the UPDATE command. Changing a value inside an existing row changes data, not structure, so a DML command is needed: UPDATE. ALTER TABLE changes columns, DROP TABLE removes the whole table, and INSERT adds a new row.

questions.stem_md: A column is declared as `CHAR(10)` and the value `Pune` (4 characters) is stored in it. How much space does MySQL keep for this value?

options.text_md: A fixed 10 characters, padded with spaces
5 characters: the value and its length
As many characters as the longest value in the column

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A fixed 10 characters, padded with spaces. CHAR(n) is fixed-length: every value occupies n characters, padded with spaces. VARCHAR(n) is variable-length and keeps only the characters actually entered (up to n).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about a **PRIMARY KEY** column of a MySQL table is correct?

options.text_md: Its values may repeat but cannot be NULL
A table may have several separate primary keys
Its values must be unique and it cannot contain NULL
It must always be the first column of the table

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Its values must be unique and it cannot contain NULL. A primary key identifies each row, so it is both UNIQUE and NOT NULL. A table has only one primary key (it may span more than one column), and its position among the columns does not matter.

questions.stem_md: Which MySQL command shows the column names, data types and keys of the table PRODUCT?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** `DESCRIBE PRODUCT;`. DESCRIBE (or DESC) shows the structure of a table. SHOW is used as SHOW DATABASES or SHOW TABLES; the other two are not SQL commands.

questions.stem_md: Meera wants to add a column `Phone` of type `CHAR(10)` to the existing STUDENT table without losing any data. Which statement should she run?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** `ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD Phone CHAR(10);`. A new column changes the structure of the table, so it needs ALTER TABLE … ADD. UPDATE changes values, INSERT adds rows and CREATE TABLE makes a new table.

questions.stem_md: Kabir runs `DELETE FROM EVENT;` and Neha runs `DROP TABLE EVENT;` on two copies of the same database. Which statement describes the two results correctly?

Kabir's command gives an error because it has no WHERE clause
Kabir is left with an empty EVENT table; Neha has no EVENT table at all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Kabir is left with an empty EVENT table; Neha has no EVENT table at all. DELETE without WHERE removes every row but keeps the table and its structure. **Assertion (A):** In MySQL, a column declared UNIQUE (but not NOT NULL) may hold NULL in more than one row.
